name: Hereditary Angioedema

criteria.description: Recurrent episodes of angioedema without urticaria, lasting >12 hours
Low C4 level (screening test; low during and often between attacks)
Low C1-INH antigenic level (Type I HAE, ~85% of cases)
Low C1-INH functional level with normal or elevated antigenic level (Type II HAE, ~15% of cases)
Family history of HAE (positive in ~75% of cases)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Compatible clinical history plus low C4 confirmed by low C1-INH antigenic or functional level on two separate occasions (at least 1 month apart)
diagnosticCriteria.notes: HAE Type III (HAE with normal C1-INH) is rare and may involve Factor XII (Hageman factor), plasminogen, or angiopoietin-1 mutations. C1q is normal in HAE (low in acquired angioedema).

pathognomonic.notes: Key distinction: NO urticaria (hives) and NO itching; edema is non-pitting

common.symptomName: Peripheral extremity swelling (hands, feet, arms, legs)
Abdominal attacks (severe cramping pain, nausea, vomiting)
common.notes: Can mimic acute abdomen; may cause unnecessary surgery if undiagnosed

occasional.notes: Life-threatening; can cause asphyxiation; leading cause of HAE-related death
Non-raised, non-pruritic serpiginous erythema preceding an attack by hours

laboratory: Low C4 level (best screening test; low during and usually between attacks)
Low C1-INH functional level (Types I and II)
Normal C1q level (distinguishes from acquired angioedema where C1q is low)
Tryptase normal (distinguishes from mast cell-mediated angioedema)
imaging: CT abdomen during abdominal attack may show bowel wall edema and ascites
Laryngoscopy during throat attacks shows supraglottic edema
genetic: SERPING1 gene mutations (Types I and II)
F12 (Factor XII) mutations in some Type III HAE
PLG (plasminogen) mutations in some Type III
ANGPT1 mutations in some Type III
Autosomal dominant inheritance; ~25% de novo mutations
other: Attack diary documenting trigger factors, duration, and location of swelling
No response to antihistamines, epinephrine, or corticosteroids (distinguishes from allergic angioedema)

distinguishingFeatures: Temporal relationship with ACE inhibitor use
Low C1q level (unlike HAE where C1q is normal)
Associated with lymphoproliferative disorders or autoimmune disease

redFlags: Laryngeal edema with stridor or voice change (airway emergency)
Severe abdominal attack mimicking surgical abdomen
Attacks triggered by dental procedures, intubation, or surgery
Worsening of attacks with estrogen-containing contraceptives or HRT
No response to standard allergy treatments (antihistamines, epinephrine, steroids)
references: Maurer M, et al. The international WAO/EAACI guideline for the management of hereditary angioedema - The 2021 revision and update. Allergy. 2022;77(7):1961-1990.
Zuraw BL. Hereditary angioedema. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(10):1027-1036.
Betschel S, et al. The International/Canadian Hereditary Angioedema Guideline. Allergy Asthma Clin Immunol. 2019;15:72.
Bork K, et al. Hereditary angioedema with normal C1-INH with versus without specific F12 gene mutations. Allergy. 2009;64(10):1427-1430.
